value: A liquid at or above 100 °C in a bulk packaging is an elevated temperature material, and the hazardous material definition takes in that group as well as the table and the class criteria.
reason: The old explanation named other groups (substances, wastes, marine pollutants) but never said why this liquid qualifies. 171.8 'Elevated temperature material' (p. 26): '(1) Is in a liquid phase and at a temperature at or above 100 °C (212 °F)'; 'Hazardous material' (p. 27) includes 'elevated temperature materials'.

value: When carrier personnel do the loading, or it is done in their presence, for the purpose of transporting the hazmat.
reason: The old back ('done for the purpose of transporting it by carrier personnel') reads as if carrier personnel do the transporting. 171.1(c)(2) (p. 3): 'Loading of packaged or containerized hazardous material onto a transport vehicle, aircraft, or vessel for the purpose of transporting it ... when performed by carrier personnel or in the presence of carrier personnel.'

value: 172.702(c) leaves the source of training open, but 172.702(a) keeps the duty to ensure that each hazmat employee is trained on the employer.
reason: 172.704(c)(4) is about compliance while training is incomplete ('regardless of whether the training required by this subpart has been completed', p. 305–306), not about who delivers it. 172.702(a) (p. 304): 'A hazmat employer shall ensure that each of its hazmat employees is trained'.

value: The skin test is the main route in; a liquid, or a solid that may become liquid in transport, is also corrosive if it has a severe corrosion rate on steel or aluminium.
reason: The old explanation offered the steel/aluminium route for any material; 173.136(a) (p. 124) limits it: 'A liquid, or a solid which may become liquid during transportation, that has a severe corrosion rate on steel or aluminum'.

value: Vapours use a different test: an LC50 of not more than 5000 mL/m3, with a saturated vapour concentration at 20 °C of at least one-fifth of that LC50.
reason: 'A high saturated vapour concentration' is vague. 173.132(a)(1)(iii)(B) (p. 115): 'saturated vapor concentration in air at 20 °C (68 °F) greater than or equal to one-fifth of the LC50 ... and with an LC50 ... of not more than 5000 mL/m3'.

value: Any two of: an elevated temperature material; a hazardous substance; a hazardous waste; a marine pollutant.
reason: 'Among others' suggests a longer list, but 173.140(b) (p. 127–128) names exactly four: 'an elevated temperature material, a hazardous substance, a hazardous waste, or a marine pollutant'.

value: A: the definition needs both the activity concentration and the total activity to exceed the values. C: containing radionuclides is not enough; both activity values must also be exceeded. D: the order ranks classes for materials with several hazards; it does not decide whether a material is Class 7.
reason: 'The definition adds the two activity tests' is hard to parse. 173.403 (p. 307): 'any material containing radionuclides where both the activity concentration and the total activity in the consignment exceed the values'.

value: A: Class 1 materials are taken out of the § 173.2a order and stay in Class 1. C: the table covers Classes 3 and 8 and Divisions 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 5.1 and 6.1, not Class 1. D: nothing in the case makes the material toxic.
reason: 'Divisions 4.1–6.1' reads as a range that takes in 5.2 and 6.2, which the precedence table does not cover. 173.2a(a)(8) (p. 6) lists Class 3, Class 8 and Divisions 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 5.1 and 6.1.

value: When a material not in the § 172.101 table or its entries for articles containing hazmat meets two or more class definitions.
reason: The old back left out the article entries. 173.2a(a) (p. 6): 'a material not specifically listed in the § 172.101 Table or assigned to an entry of articles containing hazardous materials (UN3537 to UN3548)'.

value: Class 7 heads the list; the entry leaves out limited quantities but adds uranium hexafluoride shipped as radioactive material in excepted packages.
reason: The explanation mentioned only the limited-quantity carve-out. 173.2a(a)(1) (p. 6): 'Class 7 (radioactive materials, other than limited quantities; and shipments of UN 3507, Uranium hexafluoride, radioactive material, excepted package)'.
